title: Assessing the Reliability of Persona-Conditioned LLMs as Synthetic Survey Respondents
measurement_description: The paper evaluated the alignment of Large Language Models' (LLMs) survey answers with human ground-truth responses from the World Values Survey (WVS). Specifically, it measured how persona-prompting, which included the respondent's religious denomination as an attribute, affected the model's response accuracy (Hard Similarity) and ordinal similarity (Soft Similarity) compared to a non-persona baseline. The evaluation also included several questions directly about religion, such as trust in people of other religions and attendance at religious services.
findings: Persona prompting, which included a religious attribute, did not consistently improve the alignment of LLM responses with human survey data. The effects were heterogeneous across different religious subgroups. While persona-based prompting sometimes slightly outperformed the vanilla baseline for certain religious groups, it underperformed for others. The paper highlights that performance shifts were more pronounced in smaller subgroups, indicating that demographic conditioning can redistribute error unevenly and undermine subgroup fidelity for religious and other demographic categories.
